The resolution was one, he said, which above all c there must interest the minds and feelings of Liberals. As a rcle, in the past we had paid too much attention to foreign politics. The dust duty of Englishmen was to govern England wisely and justly; the affairs of other nations were a matter of secondary interest. But there were great crises in the history of the world, when it behoved us to look beyohd ourselves. One of those crises had come now, and every E iglishman was bound to Inform his own mind and conscience as to what should be the policy of the Government in this Eastern Quelition. As Yr. Gladstone had pointed out, we could not wash our hands a the whole affair, for we ourselves were greatly answerable for the miserable condition of the oppressed provinces. Nobody could deny that if the Western nations of Europe had allowed the Russians to overrun Turkey in Europe, and to have occupied Constantinople, the condition of the Christian populations would have been far better than at present. The Powers of Western Europe, hc wever, thought fit to prevent that. But a greater obligation than any treaty could show at- tached to us to sea that theee populations should not be exposed to perpetual injustice, and to ccc isionel outbreaks of devilish ferocity, such as had been wit- nessed. He rejoiced at the emphatic protest made by the Lb.ral party in this matter, and he rejoiced still more that the protest had been so far a national one. He thought if a Liberal Governm-nt had acted as the present Government had done, the Liberal party would have come forward and censured them. Though, however, Liberals thought that the existing Govern- ment had been remiss, cold, and apathetic in dealing with this important matter, they aid not on that ac- e nut desire to make the questicn a r arty question. He desired that if possible the pr sent Cabinet, which had so far conducted the negotiations, should go on conducting them, but with their minds informed of the will of the peopk, and in a ye: y different spirit from that in which they had hitherto acted. (Cheers.) Per. lisps at the present moment there was only one member of the Cabinet who was utterly out of sympathy with, and hostile to, the feeling of the nation—the member who made a speech recently at Aylesbury, and who had been repudiated by eve, y one of the other members in all the public speeches they had made. (Hear, hear.) Hi b. heved that if the pressure of public pinion was o ulinued upon the ()abject its attilkie would be coana-d. He had no fear now that the Government wonld dare to involve England in the expenditure of one sixpence. or the firing of oae Ow in behalf of the abominable despotism which ruled Till key. But we had a responsibility in the councils of Europe, and it was important that the voice of England should in them be raised, not in favour of shrinking and timi- dity, but in favour of thorough and efficient changes which would guarantee the suffering populations in the future against all such outrages as they had been sub. j .ct to. (Rear, hear.) The Conservative press charged Libei ale with being factious and unpatriotic, and wi h hampering the Goveromeot in the conduct of the ne- gotiations. No doubt the Government had been ham- pered, and very properly in his opinion, because they were going in a course which was not what the coun- try desired. He hoped the day would never come when the people would submit to being eilencedbecam tue Government wished to embark on a policy whicti was not endorsed by the nation. (Cheers,) The Con- servative piers also alleged that those who objected to the policy of the Government ware praying into the hands of Russia. It that were so, he would far rather 8.8 the subject provinces under the Russian than the Turk. He did nct consider the Russian Government an ideal Government. It was stained with many crimes against humanity, and he did not think that leuedan dominion was the best form the future of these provinces could t ,ke. But if we did not want to have the Russians ruling them what could be more to dish than to reake their inhabitants look to the Ruse eiane as their only deliverers. The wise policy of England was to cutbid hussia in the cause of humanity and justice, and thus prevent that des. . potio Power, whose hands were red with blood, from coming forward in the attitude of liberator and friend. (Cheers.) Let the Cabinet make up their minds and if they shrank from carrying out the will of the nation in au. deavouring tcr secure for the provii cue where the Chris- tians were ma Mb ority substantial local independence of the Turkish Government, the nation would 'find out other people woo could carry out them well; but if the Cabinet acted as the people desired them to do they would be earning just applause, and no party need crow over them or charge them with a change of policy. div.p: A LYMM APPEAL CASE.

At the Cheshire Quarter Sessions, on Tuesday, Wm' Cuff, landlord of the Swan Hotel, Bucklow Hill, ap- pealed against a decision of the Ly min magistrates, who fined him some time ago for not having the sign in front of his house affixed in a conspicuous place. Mr. Swetenham appeared for the appellant, and Mr. Marshall for the respondents. The appeal was again- t a conviction made by the Lymm magistrates, under the 11th Bootion of the Licensing Ad of 1872, as amended by section 28 of the Lit of 1874. According to the terme of the cotton, every licen Aid person is compelled to have a aigu affixed to his licensed premises in a con- spicuous place, in such form as the licensing justices may direct. Some three years ago the appellant re- moved a swinging sign, which he had ea front of his premises, and substituted for it a sign underneath the top of the door, which, it was contended by the justices was not in compliance with the Act,and they fined him in the penalty of 20s. and costs. div.head: ATTEMPTED MURDER AT WIDNES,
div.p: ATTEMPTED MURDER AT WIDNES,

On Monday Joseph Ford and William Ford, his son, pilot-men, living at Widnes, were taken before Mr. E. Young, on a charge of having attempted to murdef another pilot, named Thomas Ogden, by drowning. The prosecutor was in a boat in the pursuit of his avocation, about eleven o'clock at night, when his course was intercepted by another boat, in which were the prisoners and another member of the same family, for whose apprehension a warrant has been issued. The prosecutor succeeded in getting his boat moored near the Marsh, where all reside, when the prisoners, as alleged, rushed upon Ogden, struck and beat him violently, and, in the end, threw him into the Mersey, at a spot where the water was seven feet in depth. Ogden caught hold of a projecting stone, and in that way succeeded in gaining the bank. Mr. Swift, of St. Helens, appeared to watch the interests of the accused, and at that gentleman's request bail was grantee in a heavy amount for the appearance of the accused at the Petty 6essions.

MR. RYLANDS, ON THE EASTERN QUESTION.

On Saturday evening, a tea party and demonstra- tion was .held in Burnley, to celebrate the opening of Fulledge and Bartley Reform Club. Tea was served out in Salem Congregational Schoolroom, Manchester- , road, and the subsequent meeting was held in the shed belonging to Messrs. Crabtree and Hargreaves, Parlia- ment-street Burnley Wood, at whielt from 2,000 to 3.000 persons were present. Mr. RYLLNDS, who was loudly cheered on rising i.aid we had just now another instance of that cu- tempt of public opinion, and resistance of the will of the people on the part of the Tories which during the last 60 years had driven this country almost to the point of rebellion, and oast odium upon the throne. The Government at the present time was putting a great strain upon the constitution by resisting public opinion, which hid been expressed in a remarkable manner. It had treated the great gust of indignation which had passed over the country against that in- famous Government which was holding millions of un- °happy subjeots in thraldom and wretchedness with absolute contempt. (Hear, hear.) This opinion against the Government of Turkey and its tyranny was not alone the opinion of Liberals. Many of the bishops and clergy had spoken out as Christian men ought to speak, and he was glad to find that the re were peers like Lord Bath who did not forget that they ought to be Englishmen and patriots before Tories and followers of Benjamin Disraeli. (Hear, hear.) There were, too, certain Conservative members of Parliament who in the same way had expressed an opinion against the policy of the Government, and amongst the rank and file of the Conservative party in the great towns there must be multitudes of men who, equally with Liberals, were prepared to protest against that policy. The Government, in fact, ad- mitted that they did not represent public opinion in this matter. Lard Beaconsfield, in his speech, at Ayles- bury, in wh ch there were more untruths and misre- presentations thau statements of fact—(laughter)— did at all events make one statement which was true ; he said the country did not back up the Government. ("Hear, hear," and cheers.) Were the Government prepared to bow to public opinion? Not at all. They followed the usual custom of Tory Governments with a majority. in the House of Commons —they defied public opinion so long as they could do so without danger to themselves. They did more. They insulted the people of England by telling them that they were ignorant, that they knew nothing about the matter, that they were guided by an impulsive, impolitic, and foolish enthusiasm, founded on erroneous data. They went still further. They charged the leaders of the Liberal party with stimu- lating this generous outburst of public opinion in order to promote some mean and selfish party policy; and Lord Beaconsfield, in that remarkable speeen which proved that an earl's coronet had not altered the character of Benjamin Disraeli—(cheers)—oalled the leading Liberals cosigning politicians, whose con- duct might fairly be described as "worse than any of those Bulgarian atrocities of which we had heard BO much." (A. voice; "He is a Bulgatian atrocity," and latuhter.) This disgraceful calumny was understood te be levelled at Mr. Gladstone, but that statesman would stand out in history in a different view. When the history of this period came to be written by an im- partial pen, it wouli be written that Lord Beaconsfield soiled Ms public character by mixing himself up with some of the greatest atrocities of the day, while Mr. Gladstone out of office did more than the whole of the Government of England combined to put a stop to them. (Cheers.) The Government declined to fulfil the wish of the people. A dozen gentlemen, sitting round a table in Downing street, presumed to defy public opinion, and to say that they were the people who must express the mind of England, disregarding altogether the opinion of the entire nation. (A voice: "We will show them that we are the people," and cheers.) He did not wonder that under the circum- stances there should have been a demand for an autumn session. But the Government would not ell! Parliament together. (A voice : "They dare not.") Tney dare not do so, becaum they feared the criticism that Mr. Gladstone and other leaders of the Liberal . _

party Noti,Uld make upon their policy. They did not fear that they would not have a majcrity. The Tory party, as a rule, were too sub iervient to vote against Lord Beacensfield's Government, and although some score or so of Conservative m-mb-rs might take an in- dependent course, he firmly b-lieved that the balk of the Tory members woul I continue to vote through thick and thin in support of the Government. He said this because he observed that the speeches of Tory members in the country were in many eases mere echoes of the misrepresentations, mis-statements, and f else arguments of Lord. Beaconsfield and Lord Derby. And the same tune was played by the organs of Tory public opinion, from the double bees of the Londen - Staederd down to the penny whistle of the Burnley Advert:ser. (Laughter.) We on tht not to be ear. pfiend at this, It Was only natural teat Tories, if they were true Tories, should sympathise with de- spotic Turkey, and look with great dislike upon any movement in favour of freedom; and he believed, if we had an autumnal session, lots of Tory members would get up and say "We must have confidence in Her Mai esty's G ivernment. We must trust that the Government witl do evervt'ling that it is possible to do." They would say We must avoid a Eurepoan war," as though the policy of the Liberal party was likely to produce a European war, and they would ad.l We must not play into the hands of Russia." They would stalk out that old hobgoblin of Russia, and try to frighten the House and the country into believ- ing, what they did not believe, that there was some danger that Russian intrigue and influence might be carried too far. The fact was that the Parliament of 1b74 did not fitly represent the opinion of the coun- try at the present time. (Hear, hear.) It was elected in a period of political indifference and in the belief of Tory pr imiens and profession. These promises and professions had been found to be delusione. The pro. inises had been broken, and he thought it might now be said that the Government was altogether bankrupt so far as the good opinion of the general mass of the country was concerned. (Cheers.) The Tories said they would be economical ; an t they were spending several millions of a year more than the Liberals spent. They were to repeal the income tax; they were adding one penny after another to it. They were to admini- ster the army and navy a great deal better than the Giberal Government; and they were sinking our iron- clads. (Cheers.) They were to improve the condition of the farmer; and they had mocked him by a delusive Agricultural Holdings Act. They were to have—and this was what Mr. Disraeli held before the country— a spirited foreign policy; mei they had sunk the name of England so low that it was linked with a nation whose black crimes stained the history of the world. (Cheers.) The Tory Government had proved itself to be a gigantic imposture. He was convinced that the electors would not now return the Tories to power, and his f celiac was that instead of an autumn session it Would be far better to have a dissolution of Parliament. (Cheers.) He believed they would not have a contest in Burnley in the event of a dissolution, but if they had they would win by some hundreds of votes more than they did before; and throughout the country one sent after another that was lost in 1874 would be regained to the Liberal party, and the result would be that we should have a Government established in this country representing the true voice of England, which, ft the words of Mr. Gladstone, would carry dismay to the ty- rannical power. (Hear, hear.) But Lord Beacense field would not call Parliament together until he was obliged, and he would take care not to dissolve Par- liament, wh.ch was so snbssrvient to his wishes and opinions. Waat then could we do? Were we power. less in the hands of this Government, which professed to speak for us, and yet sp )ke words which were not ours? We could do much; we had done much. (Cneers.) The people of England had their ambassa- dors at foreign courts as well as Lord Beaennsfield. Our ambassadors were the electric tsl g •aph wires and the European press, which were carrying into every eourt. in Europe the knowledge that the people of Eng. laud were holding opinions and speaking with a voice very different to the counterfeit voice of the ambassa- dors aeotedited by Lord Beaconsfield. (Hear, bear.) All Europe had heard, and many statesmen had read, Mr. Glidetone's noble appeal, and they had also read accounts of the various public meetings which had been held in England, and the consequences had been that the ambassador accredited by the Tory Government, and instructed to Fp sak in a certain tone, was known not to represent the real opinion of England; and foreign governments knew that they used not pay any re- gard to the utterances welch were not supported by iLitish public opinion. The diplomacy of the Govern- m nt was disloyal, because it was untrue to the popu- lar will: and it was unpatriotic because it sought to carry out a pi Ley of which the nation disapproved and would prevent. THE cloud continues to gather in the Fast, and it would be idle to predict when and how it will burst : whether we shall be deluged with blood, or whether the gloom will pass away, and a new era will dawn upon the oppressed regions which are threatened. '1 he instinct of self-preservation, which is the strongest instinct that the present Government has ever manifestel, prompts it to withhold from us the nature of the nego- tiations which it is carrying on, and it is a humiliating fact that we are dependent for our information on this subject upon the newspapers of St. Petersburg and Vienna, of Berlin and Constantinople. From these various newspapers, our only ministerial statements at present, we gather that Lord Derby is practically ignored .in the councils of Europe, that even the Turks, who are not quick at learning, have discovered that our elective body and our Executive are not ono, and that, in short, t,ir Henry Elliott is not Lord stratford de Redcliffe. In view, then, of the daily changes which are taking place ill the aspect of the Eastern Question, and the little influence which England is now likely to exercise in its ultimate settlement, let us dismiss, for a time, as well as w can, the consideration of the traces it is likely to leave on the map of Europe, and confine ourselves to the consideration of the changes it is like/y to make upon the political chart of our own country.

Every morning brings us half a dozen extra-parliamentary utterances of men who, belonging at present to the party in power, adopt that tone of arrogance which so often hides ti emor, but who, before long, will be addressing the same audiences with their hats in their hands. As a rule, during the autumn recess, it is the business of Tory members to tell their constituents that they did not, in the past session, hinder the pass- ing of good measures, and that in the future session they will do all they can to promote bad ones. But this autumn the programme has been altered, the old after-piece is suddenly changed, and whether they have studied the part or not, the pit and gallery come to see the actors in their new characters, and the political mountebank has to do the best he can. With few honourable exceptions, every Tory member who has spoken since the close of the session has adopted the same tone and the same language in apology of the Foreign Policy of the Government some few are more acute or more skilful than others, and kn wing that their cause is weak and indefensible, they do not waste energy in trying to defend it, but they make a dexterous flank movement, and boldly espouse and pretend to glory in a forlorn hope. But the majority are either less witty or more honest, and if conscience' or principle, or independence of judgment did not enter into politics, one might admire the adherence to party, blind it is true, and therefore apt to go astray, of politicians like Lord Lindsay and Mr. Knowles, the members for Wigan. Lord Lindsay commenced his lesson by reminding us generally of the radical re- forms in internal policy, effected by Her Majesty's Government during last session and which, in the language of auctioneers, appear to be too numerous to mention by name. In many cases, these measures were prepared so carefully before they were sub- mitted to Parliament, "that in many instances the Liberal party were struck with it, and had expressed admiration at them." No doubt, the Liberal party would be struck when a Tory government introduced a care- fully prepared measure, but would not a more astute politician than Lord Lindsay have igno ed the Liberal gesture of surprise, and thus have left unacknowleged the fact that all 1 ory measures, such as slave circu- lars and the ennobling of Queens, are not always equally carefully prepared? The iberal party being thus surprised into ad- miration for the Tory party during the sitting of Parliament, being dazzled by carefully prepared measures, and rendered actually dumb s ith amazement, what does it do, as soon as it is released from the fascinating influence? "The consequence of those good measures was that, although the Oppo- sition had not been able to find the fault they desired with the Government during the session, on certain affairs which had occurred since the House rose, they had been ,the more bitter in the cry they had raised in the country." In other words the L beral party, like the curmudgeon that it is, having been unable to And a single fault with the Government during the session, turns round dur.ng the recess, and begins abusing it, and calling it weak and incapable in its Eastern policy. What would have happened if the Liberal party had been in power at the present time ? We should either have been actually at war or prepar- ing for a gigantic European war. Happily this has been averted by our hav- ing at the head of foreign affairs "a man of sagacious judgment. calm and cold in feel- ing." And then Lord Lindsay proceeds to explain the situation, and he appears to be a kind of political Rip van Winkle, who, having slept since the outbreak of the Cri- mean war, awakes to mumble the same ii audlin rubbish about Russian designs, as was current then. And these are the modest and conciliatory words in which he bids adieu to a great nation, and presumably a friendly one :—" Beware; take care how you rouse us. You felt the roar and anger of the British lion before. Be careful how you rouse him again." Mr. Knowles, Lord Lindsay's colleague, in the representation of the classic town of Wigan, appears to have had the wind taken out of his sails by this terrible gentleman, and his contribution to Oriental literature vvas chiefly confined to a coarse and clumsy attack on Mr. Gladstone.
